question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.
Turn over a new leaf
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To begin again.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Turn over a new leaf" means to make a fresh start by changing one's behaviour or way of life for the better, leaving past mistakes behind. (नए सिरे से शुरुआत करना / सुधर जाना)
◦ Example: After failing the exam, Rohan decided to turn over a new leaf and study seriously.

• The expression comes from the literal turning of a page ("leaf") in a book to a fresh, blank page, symbolising a new beginning.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: To stop finally: This means to end something permanently, not to make a fresh start; it lacks the idea of reform or renewal contained in the idiom.

• Option 3: To plant a tree: This is the literal, non-idiomatic meaning of some of the words and is unrelated to the actual figurative sense of the idiom.

• Option 4: To take a break: This suggests a temporary pause, whereas the idiom implies a permanent change in conduct or habits, not a rest.

NOTE

• Other idioms of reform/fresh start often asked in SSC: "To bury the hatchet" (to make peace), "To wipe the slate clean" (to forget past mistakes and start afresh) and "To mend one's ways" (to improve one's behaviour).

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

A.The principal wished the students continued to aim for perfection in their future endeavours.
B.The principal also lauded educators for their tireless efforts to educate students and inspire them to come up with new ideas.
C.Our college's principal delivered an excellent speech in which he lauded the pupils.
D.The principal mentioned how teaching assistants assisted students in resolving academic and social challenges.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. CDBA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence C ("Our college's principal delivered an excellent speech in which he lauded the pupils.") is the best opening line as it introduces the subject — the principal's speech — and mentions praise for the students in general terms.

• Sentence D logically follows C because it specifies one particular point made in that speech — how teaching assistants helped students resolve academic and social challenges.

• Sentence B follows D with the connector "also" ("The principal also lauded educators...") — this word links it to the previous point about teaching assistants/educators, continuing the theme of praising staff.

• Sentence A is the best concluding line, as it expresses the principal's closing wish for the students' future, which naturally comes after all the praise and observations have been made.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (ABCD) is incorrect because it starts with the principal's closing wish (A) before the speech itself is even introduced (C), which is illogical.

• Option 3 (CABD) is incorrect because it places the concluding wish (A) immediately after the introduction (C), before the specific points made in the speech (D and B) are mentioned.

• Option 4 (DBAC) is incorrect because it begins with a specific detail (D) before the speech itself has been introduced (C), leaving the reader without context.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always identify the sentence that introduces the topic in general terms (usually the opening sentence) and the sentence that provides a natural conclusion or closing remark (usually the last sentence); then use connecting words like "also", "however", "this", "it" etc. to link the middle sentences correctly.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the given sentence.
A fair-weather friend can never be trusted in the times of exigency.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. A selfish friend.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A fair-weather friend" refers to a person who stays friendly only when things are going well, but abandons or deserts you in times of difficulty or need, thinking only of their own comfort and interest. (मतलबी दोस्त / स्वार्थी मित्र)
◦ Example: He proved to be a fair-weather friend when he refused to help me during my financial crisis.

• The idiom draws on the image of "fair weather" (good weather) — such a friend enjoys your company only in favourable, easy conditions, which is why, among the given options, "a selfish friend" best captures the self-centred, unreliable nature of such a person.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: A close friend is incorrect because it suggests genuine intimacy and loyalty, which is the opposite of what a fair-weather friend offers.

• Option 2: A pen friend is incorrect because it refers to a friend one corresponds with by letter, a completely different and unrelated concept.

• Option 4: An old acquaintance is incorrect because it merely denotes someone known for a long time, without any implication of selfishness or unreliability in hard times.

NOTE

• Other idioms about unreliable or false friendship often asked in SSC: "A wolf in sheep's clothing" (someone who appears friendly but is dangerous), "To stab someone in the back" (to betray someone who trusts you) and "A friend in need is a friend indeed" (a true friend helps in difficulty — the exact opposite of a fair-weather friend).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a grammatical error.
Bobo was / very richer than Jim / as he had illicitly accumulated / all his wealth.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. very richer than Jim.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "very richer than Jim" contains a grammatical error: the adverb "very" cannot be used to modify a comparative adjective like "richer".

• Rule — Intensifiers with comparative adjectives: Comparative degree adjectives/adverbs (words ending in "-er" or preceded by "more") are intensified using "much", "far", "still", "a lot" or "even", never "very". "Very" is used only with the positive degree (e.g., "very rich") or the superlative degree (e.g., "the very best").
◦ Correct form: Bobo was much/far richer than Jim.

• Applying the rule, the given segment should read "much richer than Jim" or "far richer than Jim" instead of "very richer than Jim".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "all his wealth." is correct as written; it is a grammatically sound noun phrase acting as the object of "accumulated".

• Option 3: "as he had illicitly accumulated" is correct as written; the Past Perfect Tense ("had accumulated") is properly used for an action completed before another past action, and "illicitly" is correctly placed before the main verb.

• Option 4: "Bobo was" is correct as written; it is a grammatically sound subject + verb combination.

NOTE

• Common intensifier errors tested by SSC: "very" wrongly used with comparatives (very better, very bigger, very taller) — always replace with "much/far/a lot"; also remember "very" is correctly used with superlatives only as "very best/very first/very last", not with ordinary comparatives.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Unemployment has become a fiery question of the day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. become a burning question.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a burning question" means a topic or issue that is currently of great importance, urgency, or interest, and is being widely discussed. (ज्वलंत मुद्दा / अति महत्वपूर्ण विषय)
◦ Example: Climate change has become a burning question for governments across the world.

• In the given sentence, "Unemployment has become a fiery question of the day" — the underlined segment must be replaced with the fixed idiomatic collocation "become a burning question", since "fiery question" is not standard, natural English usage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "become a freezing question" is incorrect; "freezing" (extremely cold) has no idiomatic connection with urgency or importance.

• Option 3: "become a furious question" is incorrect; "furious" describes extreme anger, not the sense of a pressing/urgent topic.

• Option 4: "become a flaming question" is incorrect; although "flaming" relates to fire like "burning", it is not part of the standard fixed idiom and sounds unnatural in this collocation.

NOTE

• Other fixed idiomatic collocations with "burning" often asked in SSC: "burning desire" (a very strong wish), "burning issue" (a matter of urgent importance, synonymous with "burning question") and "burning ambition" (an intense desire to achieve something).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word 'PENNILESS' from the given sentence.
Living in a house with a spacious lawn a proper parking space and a nice swimming pool is still a dream for many rich people in Mumbai.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Rich.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Penniless" means having no money at all; extremely poor. (कंगाल / निर्धन)
◦ Example: After losing his business, he was left penniless and had to depend on his relatives.

• The antonym of "penniless" is "Rich", meaning having a great deal of money or wealth. (धनवान / अमीर)

• In the given sentence, "a dream for many rich people in Mumbai" already uses the word "rich", confirming it as the exact opposite of "penniless" as used in context.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Space is incorrect; it means an empty area or extent, unrelated in meaning to wealth or poverty.

• Option 3: Spacious is incorrect; it means having ample space or roomy, again unrelated to financial status.

• Option 4: Dream is incorrect; it refers to a wish or aspiration (or images seen during sleep), not to wealth.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "penniless" often tested by SSC: destitute, impoverished, broke, indigent, bankrupt; their antonyms include affluent, wealthy, prosperous, well-off.

question:
Select the option that is similar in meaning to the underlined word.
He gave a concise explanation of the company's retirement plan.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Terse.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Concise" means giving a lot of information clearly and in a few words; brief and to the point. (संक्षिप्त)
◦ Example: The manager gave a concise summary of the quarterly results.

• The word "Terse" means using few words, brief and to the point, which makes it the closest synonym of "concise" among the given options. (संक्षिप्त / सारगर्भित)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Clear is incorrect; it means easy to understand or free from confusion, which relates to clarity, not to brevity, the key sense of "concise".

• Option 2: Verbose is incorrect; it means using more words than necessary, which is the direct opposite (antonym) of "concise".

• Option 4: Sharp is incorrect; it means keen, acute, or having a fine edge, and does not carry the sense of brevity.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "concise" often asked in SSC: succinct, brief, pithy, compact, laconic; its antonyms include verbose, wordy, prolix, lengthy.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
They all, except Shirin, were very sad / during the farewell party given / to the teacher retiring, and her / indifference were well noticed.
option_1: They all, except Shirin, were very sad
option_4: to the teacher retiring, and her
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. indifference were well noticed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "indifference were well noticed" contains a Subject-Verb Agreement error.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: A singular subject must always take a singular verb, and a plural subject must take a plural verb. "Indifference" is an uncountable/singular abstract noun, so it must be followed by the singular verb "was", not the plural "were".
◦ Correct form: ...and her indifference was well noticed.

• Applying the rule, "her indifference" (singular subject) requires "was well noticed", not "were well noticed".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "They all, except Shirin, were very sad" is correct as written; "they" is a plural subject, and words joined by "except" are excluded from the subject count, so the plural verb "were" is correctly used.

• Option 2: "during the farewell party given" is correct as written; it is a grammatically sound prepositional phrase with a correctly used past participle "given".

• Option 4: "to the teacher retiring, and her" is correct as written; it correctly uses the present participle "retiring" to modify "the teacher".

NOTE

• Commonly confused singular abstract nouns that take a singular verb despite sounding collective: indifference, information, advice, furniture, scenery, poetry, machinery — all are uncountable and always take a singular verb.

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully:
Estella had hardly heard the news (after) she began to weep.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. when.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the adverb "hardly", which conventionally pairs with the conjunction "when" (or "before"), never with "after", "while", "well" or "than".

• Rule — Hardly...when: The fixed structure is "Hardly + had + subject + past participle + ... + when + subject + verb (simple past)", used to show that one action occurred immediately after another.
◦ Example: Estella had hardly heard the news when she began to weep.

• Applying the rule, the bracketed word "(after)" must be replaced with "when" to form the grammatically correct and idiomatic structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "while" is incorrect; "while" indicates two actions happening simultaneously over a period, which does not fit the "hardly" structure that requires an immediate, sequential action.

• Option 2: "well" is incorrect; "well" is an adverb of manner/degree and cannot function as a conjunction linking the two clauses here.

• Option 3: "than" is incorrect; "than" is used for comparisons, and while it can pair with "no sooner" ("no sooner...than"), it does not pair with "hardly".

NOTE

• Similar inversion/correlative structures tested by SSC: "No sooner had...than", "Scarcely had...when", and "Hardly/Scarcely had...when" — all describe one action occurring immediately after or during another; the second clause always uses "when" (or "than" only with "no sooner").

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Accept
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Deny.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Accept" means to agree to receive, take, or believe something offered or stated. (स्वीकार करना)

• The antonym of "Accept" is "Deny", meaning to refuse to accept, admit, or acknowledge something. (अस्वीकार करना / इनकार करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Agree is incorrect; it is close in meaning to "accept" (to consent or concur), making it a synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 2: Respond is incorrect; it simply means to reply or react, and has no direct opposite relationship with "accept".

• Option 4: Confirm is incorrect; it means to state or establish something as true, which is again closer in sense to "accept" than opposite to it.

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs with "accept" often tested by SSC: accept × reject, accept × refuse, accept × decline, accept × repudiate.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I am ____________ after five years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. taking an exam.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct verb-noun collocation in English for sitting an examination is "to take an exam", not "make", "keep" or "fry" an exam.

• Rule — Fixed collocations: Certain nouns pair only with specific verbs by convention; "exam/test" conventionally collocates with the verb "take" (or "sit", in British usage), and no other verb is idiomatically correct here.
◦ Correct form: I am taking an exam after five years.

• The sentence means the speaker is appearing for an examination after a gap of five years, which is correctly expressed only by "taking an exam".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "making an exam" is incorrect; "make" does not collocate with "exam" in this sense (one can "make" a mistake or a decision, but not "make" an exam).

• Option 3: "keeping an exam" is incorrect; "keep" is not a standard collocation with "exam" in English usage.

• Option 4: "frying an exam" is incorrect; "fry" is used only in its literal culinary sense (to cook in hot oil) and has no idiomatic connection with examinations.

NOTE

• Other fixed verb-noun collocations often tested by SSC: take a decision/make a decision (both acceptable), take a risk, take a break, take care, keep a promise, keep a secret, make an effort, make a mistake.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to replace the underlined segment in the given sentence.
They spoke about the political turmoil in the state.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. talked.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "talk" correctly collocates with the preposition "about" to mean "to discuss a topic" — "talked about" is a standard, grammatically correct phrasal combination.
◦ Correct form: They talked about the political turmoil in the state.

• Rule — Verb + preposition collocation: Verbs like "say", "state" and "express" are transitive and take a direct object without the preposition "about" (e.g., "say something", "state a fact", "express an opinion"); they do not naturally combine with "about" to mean "discuss".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "expressed" is incorrect; "express" takes a direct object (e.g., "expressed their views"), and "expressed about" is not standard usage.

• Option 2: "said" is incorrect; "said" also takes a direct object or "said that...", and "said about" is not idiomatic English.

• Option 4: "stated" is incorrect; similarly, "stated" is transitive and does not collocate with "about" ("stated about" is ungrammatical).

NOTE

• Remember: "talk about", "speak about" are the correct patterns for expressing "to converse on a topic" using "about"; note that "discuss" is itself directly transitive, so "discuss about" (without "talk"/"speak") is a very common SSC error to avoid.

question:
Select the correct active form of the given sentence.
Luckily, the machinery was not used by them.
option_1: Luckily, they had not used the machinery.
option_2: Luckily, they did not use the machinery.
option_3: Luckily, they have not used the machinery.
option_4: Luckily, I did not used the machinery.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Luckily, they did not use the machinery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Luckily, the machinery was not used by them" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Past Tense (negative).

• Rule — Simple Past Tense (negative):
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + not + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + did not + V1 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "them" becomes the subject "they"; the auxiliary "was...not" is converted to "did not"; and the past participle "used" is converted to the base form "use"; the object "the machinery" becomes the object of the active sentence.
◦ Active: Luckily, they did not use the machinery.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Luckily, they had not used the machinery." is incorrect because "had not used" is the Past Perfect Tense, which does not match the Simple Past Tense of the given passive sentence.

• Option 3: "Luckily, they have not used the machinery." is incorrect because "have not used" is the Present Perfect Tense, not the Simple Past Tense.

• Option 4: "Luckily, I did not used the machinery." is incorrect for two reasons: the subject has been wrongly changed from "they" to "I", which does not correspond to the agent "them" in the original sentence; and "did not used" is grammatically wrong, since the auxiliary "did" must always be followed by the base form of the verb ("use"), not the past form "used".

NOTE

• The introductory adverb "Luckily" is a sentence modifier and remains unchanged when converting between active and passive voice — only the core clause changes. Also remember: after the auxiliary "did/did not" in the Simple Past Tense, the main verb always stays in its base (V1) form.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank and complete the collocation.
Happiness can be spread by being grateful or ________ compliments to someone.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. paying.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct verb-noun collocation is "to pay a compliment" or "to pay compliments", meaning to say something nice or praise someone.

• Rule — Fixed collocations: "Compliment(s)" is idiomatically paired only with the verb "pay" in standard English usage, not with "give", "accept" or "share".
◦ Correct form: Happiness can be spread by being grateful or paying compliments to someone.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "giving" is incorrect; although "give" is a common verb of transfer, it does not form the idiomatic fixed collocation with "compliments" that is standard in English.

• Option 3: "accepting" is incorrect; "accepting compliments" means receiving them, which reverses the intended meaning — here the speaker is offering, not receiving, praise.

• Option 4: "sharing" is incorrect; "sharing compliments" is not an established English collocation.

NOTE

• Other fixed collocations with "pay" often tested by SSC: pay attention, pay a visit, pay heed, pay respect, pay a price, pay tribute.

question:
Parts of the given sentence have been given as options. One of them contains a spelling error. Select the option that rectifies the error.
In research done by an online publecation it was found that the most popular password is 123456!
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. publication.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Publication" — meaning the act of publishing, or a published work such as a book, journal, or magazine. (प्रकाशन)
◦ Example: The research findings appeared in a well-known scientific publication.

• Spelling key: PUB + LI + CA + TION. The word given in the passage, "publecation", incorrectly replaces the "i" in "publi-" with an "e".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "password" is spelt correctly as given in the passage; no error here.

• Option 3: "research" is spelt correctly as given in the passage; no error here.

• Option 4: "popular" is spelt correctly as given in the passage; no error here.

NOTE

• Words ending in "-ication" are frequently misspelt in SSC exams by wrongly inserting an "e": e.g., communication, application, education, dedication, indication — always check that the vowel before "-cation" is "i", not "e".

question:
Select the correct active form of the given sentence.
You are asked to tell the plumber to mend all the pipes.
option_1: Command the plumber mending all the pipes.
option_2: Tell the plumber to mend all the pipes.
option_3: All the pipes must be mend.
option_4: Tell the plumber mending all the pipes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Tell the plumber to mend all the pipes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "You are asked to tell the plumber to mend all the pipes" is the Passive form of an Imperative sentence.

• Rule — Passive of Imperative sentences:
◦ Active (Imperative): Verb (base form) + Object
◦ Passive: You are + requested/asked/ordered + to + Verb + Object

• Applying the rule in reverse, the passive phrase "You are asked to tell..." is converted back to the direct command form by simply dropping "You are asked to" and starting with the base verb.
◦ Active: Tell the plumber to mend all the pipes.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Command the plumber mending all the pipes." is incorrect; it changes the meaning of the sentence (introducing "command") and uses a grammatically wrong non-finite form "mending" instead of the infinitive "to mend".

• Option 3: "All the pipes must be mend." is incorrect; it is passive in structure ("must be mend") and also grammatically wrong, as the correct passive of a modal verb requires the past participle "mended", not "mend".

• Option 4: "Tell the plumber mending all the pipes." is incorrect; it incorrectly uses the gerund/participle "mending" instead of the infinitive "to mend", changing the intended meaning.

NOTE

• Remember the standard passive forms of imperative sentences: "Let + object + be + V3" (for simple commands) and "You are requested/advised/ordered/asked + to + V1" (for polite commands or requests) — both are frequently tested by SSC.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Holding on to something or keeping an opinion with determination
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Tenacious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Tenacious" means holding firmly to something, or persistently maintaining an opinion, course of action, or belief with determination. (दृढ़ / हठी / मजबूती से पकड़े रहने वाला)
◦ Example: Despite repeated setbacks, she remained tenacious in pursuing her goal.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Gracious (विनम्र/उदार) means courteous, kind, and pleasant, unrelated to holding on to something with determination.

• Option 3: Obnoxious (घृणित) means extremely unpleasant or objectionable, which has no connection with determination or persistence.

• Option 4: Loquacious (बातूनी) means talking a great deal; excessively talkative, which is unrelated to firmness of opinion.

NOTE

• Other one-word substitutions related to persistence/determination often tested by SSC: Adamant (refusing to change one's mind), Obstinate (stubbornly refusing to change), Persevering (continuing steadily despite difficulty), Resolute (firm and determined).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a grammatical error. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
Her concerts / are very admired / by the foreigners / no error.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. are very admired.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "are very admired" contains a grammatical error in the use of the intensifier "very" with the past participle "admired".

• Rule — Intensifiers with past participles used passively: When a past participle (like "admired", "impressed", "surprised") functions as part of a passive verb, it should be intensified using "much", "greatly" or "highly", not "very", unless the participle has become a pure adjective (e.g., "very tired", "very interested").
◦ Correct form: Her concerts are much/greatly admired by the foreigners.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "by the foreigners." is correct as written; it is a properly formed agentive phrase in the passive voice.

• Option 3: "No error" is incorrect as an answer choice because an error does exist in segment 1, as explained above.

• Option 4: "Her concerts" is correct as written; it is a grammatically sound subject phrase.

NOTE

• Common SSC trap: distinguishing between participial adjectives that take "very" (very tired, very bored, very excited, very interested) and passive verb forms that require "much/greatly/highly" (much admired, greatly influenced, highly appreciated) — when in doubt, check whether the word functions as a true adjective or as part of a passive verb describing an action done by an agent.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Sinhaleese.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Sinhalese" — referring to the majority ethnic group of Sri Lanka, or their language.

• Spelling key: SINHA + LESE. The given option "Sinhaleese" wrongly inserts an extra "e" before the final "se", producing "-leese" instead of the correct "-lese".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Sabbatical" is spelt correctly; it means a period of paid leave, typically for study or travel, granted to a university teacher or other worker.

• Option 2: "Confluence" is spelt correctly; it means the junction of two rivers, or a coming together of people or things.

• Option 4: "Conform" is spelt correctly; it means to comply with rules, standards, or expectations.

NOTE

• Words ending in "-ese" (denoting nationality/language, e.g., Chinese, Japanese, Portuguese, Sinhalese, Vietnamese, Burmese) are commonly misspelt by SSC candidates with an extra vowel before the ending — always double-check that only a single "e" precedes the final "se".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word vivid from the given sentence:
In my murky memory lane, I still could vividly apprehend and envision the pictures of Nischindipu while reading Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay's “Pather Panchali”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. murky.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Vivid" means producing powerful feelings or clear, sharp images in the mind; bright and intense. (स्पष्ट / जीवंत)

• The antonym of "vivid" is "Murky", meaning dark and gloomy; unclear, obscure, or difficult to see through. (धुंधला / अस्पष्ट)

• In the given sentence, "In my murky memory lane, I still could vividly apprehend..." already contrasts "murky" (unclear) with "vividly" (clearly), confirming "murky" as the direct opposite of "vivid".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Perceive is incorrect; it is a verb meaning to become aware of or notice something, and is a near-synonym in context of clearly grasping something, not an antonym.

• Option 2: Apprehend is incorrect; here it means to understand or grasp mentally, which is close in sense to "vividly" perceiving something rather than its opposite.

• Option 4: Envision is incorrect; it means to imagine or picture something clearly in the mind, which again aligns with, rather than opposes, the sense of "vivid".

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs with "vivid" often tested by SSC: vivid × dull, vivid × pale, vivid × faint, vivid × hazy, vivid × colourless.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The thing nodded vigorously; as it nodded, the left button-eye fell off and (1) ________ (2) ________ the concrete floor. The thing looked around (3) ________ with its one eye, as if it had lost her. The thing twisted bonelessly (4) ________ its one eye was again facing her. And it (5) ________ across the cellar towards her then.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. clattered.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "clattered" describes a loud rattling noise made by hard objects striking a hard surface — exactly the sound a small hard button-eye would make falling onto a concrete floor.

• The context — a button-eye falling off and hitting a "concrete floor" — calls for a verb describing an abrupt, sharp, knocking sound, which "clattered" precisely conveys.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "hissed" is incorrect; "hiss" describes a sharp sibilant sound like escaping steam or gas, or a snake's sound, not the noise of a hard object striking a floor.

• Option 3: "fizzed" is incorrect; "fizz" describes the sound of small bubbles of gas escaping (like a fizzy drink), which does not match a hard object falling.

• Option 4: "buzzed" is incorrect; "buzz" describes a continuous humming or vibrating sound, such as that made by an insect or an electrical device, not a single impact sound.

NOTE

• Onomatopoeic verbs commonly tested by SSC in cloze passages: clattered, banged, thudded, crashed (sounds of impact); hissed, buzzed, whirred, fizzed (continuous or sibilant sounds) — always choose the verb that matches the specific physical action described in the passage.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. on to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "clattered on to the concrete floor" requires a preposition indicating movement towards and landing upon a surface — "on to" (onto) correctly expresses this sense of falling and coming to rest on the floor.

• Rule — Prepositions of movement and position: "On to"/"onto" combines the idea of motion ("to") with final position ("on"), making it the natural choice for something that falls and lands on a surface.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "up" is incorrect; "up" indicates upward direction, which contradicts the downward motion of the eye falling off and hitting the floor.

• Option 2: "to" is incorrect; "to" alone indicates direction towards a destination but does not capture the sense of landing/resting upon a surface as clearly as "on to".

• Option 3: "at" is incorrect; "at" indicates a fixed point or location, not the motion of something falling and coming to rest on a surface.

NOTE

• Commonly confused prepositions of movement/position tested by SSC: into (movement to the inside of something), on to/onto (movement to a position on top of something), at (a specific point), in (enclosed position) — always match the preposition to the exact type of motion or position described.

The thing twisted bonelessly (4) ________ its one eye was again facing her. And it (5) ________ across the cellar towards her then.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. until.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The conjunction "until" (or "till") means up to the point in time when something happens, and is used to show that an action continues up to a certain moment.

• The sentence "The thing twisted bonelessly ________ its one eye was again facing her" describes a continuous twisting motion that carries on up to the point when the eye faces her again — this exactly matches the meaning of "until".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "unless" is incorrect; "unless" means "if not" and introduces a condition, not a point in time up to which an action continues.

• Option 3: "ever after" is incorrect; this phrase typically means "for all time after a certain point" (as in "happily ever after") and does not fit grammatically as a subordinating conjunction here.

• Option 4: "even so" is incorrect; it is a conjunctive adverb meaning "nevertheless" or "despite that", used to show contrast between two independent statements, not to link a continuing action to its end-point.

NOTE

• Commonly confused conjunctions tested by SSC: until/till (up to a point in time), unless (a negative condition), as long as (during the time that), by the time (before a specified point) — always check whether the sentence needs a condition, a contrast, or a time-limit.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. lunged.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "lunged" means made a sudden forceful forward movement, which fits the dramatic, threatening action of "it" moving across the cellar towards her.

• The sentence "And it ________ across the cellar towards her then" describes a sudden, aggressive forward motion, which is best conveyed by "lunged" among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "hung" is incorrect; "hung" (past tense of "hang") describes suspension from above, not forward movement across a space.

• Option 2: "rung" is incorrect; "rung" is the past participle of "ring" (as in a bell) or refers to a step of a ladder; neither fits the sense of sudden forward movement.

• Option 4: "flung" is incorrect; "flung" (past tense of "fling") means to throw something forcefully, and requires an object being thrown — it does not describe the subject's own forward bodily movement in this context.

NOTE

• Verbs describing sudden forceful movement often tested by SSC in narrative cloze passages: lunged, pounced, sprang, darted, charged — distinguish these from verbs of suspension (hung), sound (rung), or throwing (flung), which are common distractor options with similar spellings/sounds.
